about: Where to find a doctor who knows POTS, and people who get it — organisations run by patients or clinicians only. Splyt does not list or recommend individual doctors. Every link was opened and read by a person on the date shown. Free to reuse under CC BY 4.0; please credit splyt.fit/pots/help.

needs.label: Getting diagnosed
needs.line: Where to start if you think it’s POTS — what it is, and how it’s tested.

needs.label: A doctor who knows POTS
needs.line: Lists kept by patient organisations. Read how each one is made — none of them can vouch for every name on it.

needs.label: People who get it
needs.line: Groups run by people who live with POTS too.

needs.label: After COVID
needs.line: If this started after COVID, these are the services and charities for long COVID.

needs.label: Supporting someone
needs.line: For partners, parents and friends — what to read, and where to find others doing the same.

needs.label: Getting ready for an appointment
needs.line: What to bring, so it isn’t your memory against the clock.

entries.name: Dysautonomia International — Find a Doctor
entries.what: Doctors who see POTS, kept by the largest patient organisation.
entries.how: Doctors ask to be listed and Dysautonomia International reviews them. It says plainly it isn’t a complete list — call before you book.

entries.name: Dysautonomia Support Network — provider map
entries.what: A map of providers that people with dysautonomia have recommended.
entries.how: Built from patient recommendations, not checked or endorsed by the network, and it includes some integrative providers — ask what testing they do.

entries.name: Standing Up to POTS — finding an autonomic doctor
entries.what: What an autonomic specialist is, and the lists to look in for one.
entries.how: A patient-run charity. It points to other organisations’ lists rather than keeping its own.

entries.name: PoTS UK — NHS clinics
entries.what: The NHS clinics that see PoTS, gathered by the UK charity.
entries.how: NHS clinics only, and not an endorsement. You’ll usually need a referral from your GP.

entries.name: PoTS UK — a guide for your GP
entries.what: Written for GPs. PoTS UK suggests taking it to your appointment and asking for a stand test.

entries.name: PoTS UK — online peer support groups
entries.what: Online groups for adults, 13–17 year olds, parents, the newly diagnosed, men, and Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales.
entries.how: Free; you book a place through Eventbrite.

entries.name: NHS — PoTS
entries.what: The NHS page: symptoms, how it’s diagnosed, and what to ask your GP.

entries.name: NHS — long COVID
entries.what: Symptoms that last after COVID, and getting help through your GP.

entries.name: Long Covid Support
entries.what: A UK charity run by people with long COVID: peer support and advocacy.

entries.name: Australian POTS Foundation — clinician directory
entries.what: Clinicians in Australia who see POTS.
entries.how: Clinicians list themselves as members of the Foundation, which says it does not screen or endorse them.

entries.name: Australian POTS Foundation
entries.what: The Australian patient organisation: information, events and support.

entries.name: Complex Chronic Illness Support
entries.what: A New Zealand charity for people with complex chronic illness, including POTS and long COVID, and their families.

entries.name: Healthify — POTS
entries.what: New Zealand’s health information page on POTS.

entries.name: Healthify — POTS support
entries.what: Where to find support in New Zealand.

entries.name: PoTS und andere Dysautonomien e.V.
entries.what: The German-speaking patient organisation: information, a checklist for testing, and community.
entries.how: In German. It doesn’t keep a list of doctors.

entries.name: PoTS e.V. — Online-Treffs
entries.what: Online meet-ups with other people who have POTS.

entries.name: Long COVID — Bürgertelefon & regional clinic search
entries.what: The German health ministry’s long COVID phone line and a search for clinics near you.

entries.name: DIT IS POTS — where to go for diagnosis or treatment
entries.what: Specialists in the Netherlands and Belgium that people with POTS have been seen by.
entries.how: In Dutch. Gathered from patients’ experiences, with no date on it — check a doctor still sees POTS before you’re referred.

entries.name: DIT IS POTS
entries.what: A patient-run platform for people with POTS in the Netherlands and Belgium.

entries.name: 1177 — POTS
entries.what: Sweden’s public health guide on POTS: symptoms, tests, and where to get care.

entries.name: Dysautonomi Sverige
entries.what: A Swedish site about dysautonomia, made by people who live with it.

entries.name: Dysautonomia International — support groups
entries.what: Volunteer-run groups by US state and by country, including Canadian provinces, India and Australia.
entries.how: Mostly Facebook groups, run by people who have POTS.

entries.name: Dysautonomia Support Network — regional communities
entries.what: Peer communities by US region.

entries.name: Dysautonomia International
entries.what: The largest patient organisation for POTS and other forms of dysautonomia: information, research and awareness.

entries.name: Standing Up to POTS
entries.what: A patient-run charity: explainers made with clinicians, a podcast, and community.

entries.name: Cleveland Clinic — POTS
entries.what: A clear clinical overview: what POTS is, how it’s diagnosed and treated.

entries.name: Standing Up to POTS — preparing for the doctor
entries.what: The best preparation guide we found: what to track, what to bring, and how to make the time count.

entries.name: Dysautonomia International — patient advocacy tips
entries.what: How to speak up for yourself in appointments — and what to do when you’re not being heard.

entries.name: Dysautonomia International — wallet cards
entries.what: Printable cards that explain POTS and the accommodations you need — for school, work or the emergency room.

entries.name: Dysautonomia Support Network — handbooks and handouts
entries.what: Free handouts to give to family, teachers and doctors.
